topics.title: Greetings
topics.description: Say hello, goodbye, and how are you

guide.intro: Mandarin has only a handful of greetings to learn — but the tones really matter. Here's what to know before you start.

sections.text: The four tones

Every Mandarin syllable has one of four pitched tones (plus a neutral "fifth" tone). The same syllable means different things depending on tone — so "mā", "má", "mǎ", and "mà" are four different words.
Hello: 你好 (nǐ hǎo)
你 means "you" and 好 means "good". Put them together for "you good?" — the standard hello, usable any time of day.
When two 3rd-tone syllables stack like nǐ hǎo, the first one shifts up to a 2nd tone in speech (ní hǎo). It still gets written as nǐ hǎo.
你 (nǐ) vs 您 (nín)
您 is the polite form of "you" — used with elders, customers, and strangers. 你 is everyday/casual. Both pronounced almost the same.
How are you?
To turn a statement into a yes/no question, just add 吗 (ma) at the end. So 你好 ("you're good") + 吗 = 你好吗? ("are you good?").

topics.title: Numbers
topics.description: Count, ask how many, give your age

guide.intro: Mandarin numbers are wonderfully regular — once you know 1 to 10 and the word for "ten", you can build every number up to 99.

sections.text: One to ten
Building 11–99
After ten, numbers are built like math problems. Read characters left to right, multiplying anything before 十 and adding anything after.
Same trick goes further: 一百 (one hundred), 一千 (one thousand), 一万 (ten thousand) — but Chinese groups large numbers in 万 (10,000) rather than thousands.
Two: 二 vs 两
Mandarin has two words for "two". 二 (èr) is the digit — used in counting, math, and phone numbers. 两 (liǎng) means "a pair of" — used before measure words and quantities.
Asking how many
几 (jǐ) asks "how many?" for small expected counts (under ~10). 多少 (duō shǎo) asks "how much/many?" for any quantity, including money and big numbers.

topics.title: Basics
topics.description: Yes, no, I, you, this, that

guide.intro: Mandarin has no verb conjugation, no plural endings, no genders, and no articles. Once you know the word order, the language gets out of your way.

sections.text: Word order: subject – verb – object
Just like English, a basic sentence puts the subject first, the verb second, and the object last.
Pronouns are simple
他 (he) and 她 (she) are pronounced exactly the same — only the writing changes. In speech, listeners use context.
The verb 是 (shì)
是 means "to be" — but only for nouns connecting to other nouns ("I am a student"). For adjectives, you don't use 是; you use 很 (hěn) instead, which means "very" but is often a placeholder.
Negation: 不 vs 没
Use 不 (bù) for negating present and future actions, and for adjectives. Use 没 (méi) for past actions and for the verb 有 ("to have").

rows.source: 我 不 喝 茶。
我 没 有 钱。

sections.text: No tenses!
Mandarin verbs do not change form for past, present, or future. Time is shown by adding a time word (yesterday, tomorrow) or particles like 了 (le) for completion.

rows.source: 昨天 我 吃 米饭。
明天 我 吃 米饭。

exercises.explanation: "不是" literally "is not" — a common way to say "no".
Add "们" to make a plural pronoun: 我们 = we.

exercises.answer: 这 是 我 妈妈
这 是 我 爸爸

topics.title: Common verbs
topics.description: Go, eat, want, like, see, listen

guide.intro: Mandarin verbs never change form. The same character is used for all persons and all times — context (and time words) does the heavy lifting.

sections.text: One verb, every form
Compare with English: "go / goes / went / will go" — Mandarin uses 去 for all of them. The action stays put; you add words around it.
Want vs. would-like: 要 / 想 / 喜欢
These three look interchangeable in English but have a clear pecking order in Mandarin.

rows: I want / I will (decisive, ordering food)
I would like / I am thinking about

rows.source: 我 想 喝 咖啡。
rows.translation: I would like to drink coffee.

sections.text: Completion: the 了 particle
Adding 了 (le) after a verb signals an action is finished. It's the closest thing Mandarin has to past tense — but it's really an aspect marker, not a tense.

rows.source: 我 吃 了 饭。

sections.text: Don't sprinkle 了 everywhere — for adjectives ("I am happy") or stative verbs, you don't use it. Save it for completed actions.

exercises.answer: 我 有 一 个 妹妹
exercises.explanation: "个" is the most common measure word.

topics.title: Time
topics.description: Days, hours, and when things happen

guide.intro: Time words go at the start of a sentence or right after the subject — never at the end like English. "Tomorrow I go" is the natural Mandarin order.

sections.text: Days are math
Days of the week are 星期 (xīngqī, "week") + the digit. So 星期一 is week-1 (Monday), 星期二 is week-2 (Tuesday), and so on through 星期六. Sunday is the odd one out: 星期天 or 星期日.
Telling time
Hours use 点 (diǎn, "o'clock"), minutes use 分 (fēn). Half-past is 半 (bàn). "Quarter" is 一刻 (yí kè) for :15 and 三刻 for :45.
Time-words come first
In Mandarin, time goes before the verb. Compare:

rows.source: 我 明天 去 学校。
rows.translation: I am going to school tomorrow.

rows.source: 他 今天 不 来。

sections.text: A handy memory trick: Chinese says time in big-to-small order — year, month, day, hour, minute. The opposite of how dates are spoken in English.

exercises.prompt: What does "星期一" (xīng qī yī) mean?

exercises.answer: 我 现在 在 吃 饭

guide.intro: Mandarin questions are unusually friendly to learners — there's no auxiliary "do/does", no inversion. The word order stays the same as a statement.

sections.text: The 吗 particle
For yes/no questions, take a statement and add 吗 (ma) at the end. That's it. No reordering, no auxiliary verb.

rows.source: 你 喝 茶 吗？

sections.text: Question words stay put
For information questions (who, what, where), put the question word exactly where the answer would go. No fronting like English.
Common question words
A-not-A questions
A second way to ask yes/no questions: repeat the verb with 不 between. It's a touch more direct than 吗.

rows.source: 你 是不是 学生？
rows.translation: Are you a student or not?
Do you drink tea or not?

sections.text: Don't mix patterns: 你是不是学生吗？ is wrong. Pick one of the two question forms.
